newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels braces for massive march for jobs.
newsitem.headline: Brussels braces for massive march for jobs.

text.p: An estimated 100,000 labour unionists are expected descend on Brussels on Sunday for a mass protest against Europe's running sore of unemployment and apparent government indifference to the plight of the jobless.
Police said 23 special trains and 500 coaches had already been booked in Belgium alone for Sunday's March for Jobs.

Unions said they also expected thousands to come from France, with other delegations due from Spain, Portugal, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Austria, Hungary, Slovenia and the Czech Republic.

As the march, due to start at 1400 (1300 GMT), snakes its way from Brussels North Station past the bourse to South Station it will be under the watchful eyes of 600 policemen and gendarmes who are hoping for calm but are preparing for the worst.

"There will be some discreet checks on people arriving for the demonstration before they get to Brussels just to make sure there are no troublemakers," a police spokesman said on Friday. "People will be coming to march for work, not have a fight."
Medical teams will be on standby.

The unemployment rate in the 15-nation European Union remains stubbornly high at 10.8 percent of the workforce, with most governments apparently unable to tackle the festering social sore as they focus on slashing costs to prepare for joining the bloc's single currency in 1999.

Belgium has been shaken since the announcement in January of the closure of steelmaker Forges de Clabecq with the threatened loss of 1,800 jobs, and the more recent decision by French carmaker Renault to shut its Belgian plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
There have been sporadic protests and marches in Brussels and elsewhere because of the Clabecq closure.
The employment issue took on international proportions and a diplomatic dimension when Renault suddenly announced at the end of February it would close its plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde, condemned the decision, and the Belgian Federal and Flemish regional governments said they would take Renault to court.
Renault, under fire from all sides, made matters worse by refusing to reverse its decision and declaring it would also shed more than 2,700 jobs in France this year.
French Socialist Party chief Lionel Jospin will lead a delegation from national party headquarters and Communist party leader Robert Hue will take charge of his own group.
Louis Viannet, communist-led CGT union chief, and Marc Blondel, head of the non-partisan FO, will also attend.
But the issue is far wider than the bankruptcy of one company or the strategic decisions of another.

The unions want consultations with employers on issues such as working hours, and for governments to cut the indirect tax costs of employment -- both of which were key elements in the EU's 1993 White Paper, Growth, Competitiveness and Employment.

At the European level they want tax policies that encourage jobs rather than capital, a coherent social policy, moves to encourage economic growth instead of budget belt tightening, and promotion of better public services.
For their part, European governments find their hands tied by self-applied bonds.

With the decision day on who will be in the vanguard of nations joining the single currency now less than a year away, countries are slashing their expenditure -- and with it their public services -- and raising taxes in a bid to join the club.
Pundits say that such are the stakes that a failure to go ahead with the single currency, or even a delay, could prove fatal to the European Union itself.
